title: Financial Domain Basics
html:
Financial Domain Basics

Enough vocabulary and enough of the rules to model financial data without getting the arithmetic wrong. Written generically - these concepts are common to the whole industry.

Instruments

A tradable thing. The families behave differently enough that they rarely share one model:

  • Equity - ownership in a company. Priced per share. Pays dividends.
  • Bond - a loan. Has a face value, a coupon rate, a maturity date, and is usually quoted as a percentage of face rather than as an amount. Accrues interest continuously between coupon dates.
  • Fund - a holding of other instruments, priced by net asset value.
  • Derivative - value derived from something else. Adds expiry and often leverage.

The quotation basis matters more than it sounds. A bond priced at 98.5 means 98.5% of face value, so a holding of one million face is worth 985,000 - not 98.5. Treating the two the same is a classic and expensive error.

Positions and valuation

A position (or holding) is how much of an instrument an account owns at a point in time. Valuing it needs a price and, if the instrument is in another currency, a rate:

market value = quantity x price x (contract size)   ... in the instrument's currency
base value   = market value x fx rate               ... in the account's reporting currency

Unrealised gain is the difference between market value and book cost while you still hold it; realised is what is locked in when you sell. Reports distinguish them, and conflating them misstates performance.

Accrued interest on a bond is earned but unpaid income. It has to be tracked separately from the price, because the price is quoted clean - without accrual - while the amount you actually pay is dirty, with it.

Trade lifecycle

Order, execution, confirmation, settlement. Two dates matter and they are not the same:

  • Trade date - when the deal was agreed. This is when the economics change.
  • Settlement date - when cash and instrument actually change hands, typically one or two business days later.

So a position can be economically owned but not yet settled, and cash can be committed but not yet paid. Systems that use one date for both produce reconciliation breaks. The industry moved from three days to two to, in places, one, which shrinks the window in which errors can be corrected.

Trades carry a status through this lifecycle, and cancelled trades remain in the record rather than being deleted - so almost every query over trades needs a status filter, and forgetting one is a common source of overstated volumes.

Money arithmetic

Never use binary floating point for money. 0.1 is not representable, errors accumulate, and totals fail to reconcile by amounts that are impossible to explain. Use a decimal type, or integer minor units.

Decide and document the rounding rule and the scale per currency. Currencies do not all have two decimal places. Rounding at different points in a calculation gives different totals, and a report that disagrees with another report by one penny will cost more time than it deserves.

Reconciliation

Comparing your record against an external one - a custodian's positions, a bank's cash balances - and explaining every difference. Differences are normal: timing, fees, corporate actions applied on different dates. The requirement is that each is explained, not that there are none.

This is why financial systems are so date-heavy. "What did we think the position was, as at this date, as known on that date" is a routine question, and answering it needs both the business date and the knowledge date.

Corporate actions

Events changing an instrument or a holding: dividends, splits, mergers, name changes. They adjust positions and sometimes historical prices, which is why a price series has to record whether it is adjusted. Comparing an adjusted series with an unadjusted one produces a performance number that is simply wrong.

Common mistakes

  • Floating point for monetary amounts.
  • One date where trade date and settlement date are both needed.
  • Ignoring the quotation basis, and valuing a percentage-quoted bond as an amount.
  • Aggregating across currencies without converting.
  • Forgetting the status filter, and counting cancelled trades.
